title: Russia after shock therapy
body: In the 1990s Russia moved suddenly from a state-controlled economy to a market economy. About 90 per cent of its industries were put up for sale to private individuals and companies, and because the restructuring was left to market forces rather than to government-directed industrial policy, entire industries virtually disappeared. Valuable enterprises were undervalued and sold at throwaway prices. Every citizen received vouchers to take part in the sales, but most people sold their vouchers on the black market because they needed money. The value of the ruble fell sharply and inflation was so high that people lost their savings. The collective farm system broke down, leaving people without food security, and Russia began to import food. By 1999 Russia's real GDP was below its 1989 level, and about half of its 1,500 banks and financial institutions had gone bankrupt.

title: Indian films in Uzbekistan
body: Several years after the Soviet Union collapsed, a BBC correspondent reported from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, that the passion for Indian films had not faded. A shopkeeper near one of the city's biggest markets said that he sold about a hundred videos a day and estimated that most people in Tashkent bought Indian films; he explained the popularity by saying that Uzbeks are Central Asians who share a common culture with Asia. An official of the Indian embassy said that ministers and other dignitaries always mentioned Indian films in conversation, that Raj Kapoor was a household name, and that many local people could sing Hindi songs with the correct pronunciation even when they did not know the meaning. He said that almost all his neighbours could sing and play Hindi songs, which had surprised him when he arrived.
